title: After Orbán, Vučić falls: can Serbia’s students herald a new dawn for the Balkans?
gist: Serbia's Student List won over 53% and about 140 of 250 seats, ending Vučić's twelve years in power on near-70% turnout, six months after Orbán's defeat. Chatham House expects continuity on Russia (no sanctions, neutrality, gas deal and NIS refinery dependence) and EU accession still blocked by sanctions and Kosovo, with the main risk being the inexperienced movement's ability to govern.

insights.claim: Serbia's Student List won more than 53 percent of the vote and about 140 of 250 parliamentary seats at a snap election, with turnout near 70 percent, the highest since Yugoslavia's break-up in 1992; President Vučić conceded after twelve years of dominance.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: A decisive, high-turnout mandate lowers the risk of a contested transition and gives Serbian assets a cleaner political baseline.

insights.claim: A second European populist strongman in 2026 has conceded defeat after expecting to win, following Orbán in Hungary six months earlier, suggesting entrenched incumbents can lose to broad anti-incumbent coalitions.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Reduces the assumption that illiberal incumbents in Europe are unassailable; watch other long-tenured leaders for similar vulnerability.
insights.quote: For the second time this year, a European populist
insights.locator: Six months after Viktor Orbán's defeat

insights.claim: Vučić's rule ended because a leaderless student protest movement, triggered by the 2024 Novi Sad railway station canopy collapse that killed 16 and became a symbol of perceived corruption, grew into a national electoral force within two years.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Infrastructure failures that crystallise corruption perceptions can convert into regime-threatening movements; a template for monitoring procurement-linked grievance elsewhere.
insights.locator: History was born in a railway station

insights.claim: The Student List has ruled out sanctions on Russia, pledged military neutrality and rejected NATO membership, so Serbia's balancing foreign policy toward Moscow is expected to continue despite the change of government.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Do not price a sharp geopolitical pivot in Belgrade; continuity of non-alignment is the base case.
insights.quote: The Student List has explicitly ruled out sanctions against Moscow

insights.claim: Vučić's stance toward Moscow was more ambiguous than Russian praise implied: Serbia defended Ukraine's territorial integrity including Crimea and supplied Ukrainian forces with Serbian ammunition, while refusing EU sanctions.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Serbia's real alignment was already hedged, so the loss to Moscow is less material than the headline suggests.

insights.claim: Serbia depends on Russia for about 2.2 billion cubic metres of gas a year at favourable prices under an agreement expiring in December, and Russian companies hold a majority of NIS, which runs Serbia's only oil refinery; a renewal of the gas deal cannot be excluded.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Energy dependence constrains any new government's room to break with Moscow; the December gas renewal is a near-term catalyst to monitor.
insights.quote: A renewal of the existing Russian gas agreement, which expires in December, cannot be excluded at this stage.

insights.claim: The Kremlin has adopted a careful tone toward the new Serbian leadership, signalling a wish to keep good relations, and Moscow's diplomatic backing over Kosovo, including a possible UN veto or abstention, is unlikely to be ignored by the next government.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Kosovo diplomacy gives Russia leverage that keeps Belgrade from fully tilting West.

insights.claim: Serbia's EU accession has been effectively stalled for almost five years, and in July eight member states blocked opening another negotiating cluster citing democratic backsliding and insufficient foreign policy alignment.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Baseline for judging whether the new government can unlock accession momentum.
insights.locator: A new opening for Serbia's EU accession talks?

insights.claim: The new Serbian government could restore EU momentum, as in Hungary, through reforms of the judiciary, public procurement and media freedom.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Watch for early reform legislation in these three areas as the signal that accession talks can reopen.
insights.locator: A new opening for Serbia's EU accession talks?

insights.claim: Refusal to join EU sanctions against Russia and the Student List's rejection of Kosovo's independence against Brussels' demand for normalisation with Pristina remain the main obstacles to Serbian EU accession even under a reformist government.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Accession progress is likely to be slower than the political change implies; do not extrapolate Hungary's trajectory fully.
insights.quote: The stumbling stone, however, would remain Belgrade’s refusal to join European sanctions against Russia.
insights.locator: A new opening for Serbia's EU accession talks?

insights.claim: The Student List's cautious foreign policy reflects its big-tent coalition of pro-European liberals and conservative nationalists, though surveys suggest three-quarters of its supporters favour closer ties with the EU over Russia.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Coalition heterogeneity caps foreign policy ambition now, but public opinion leans West over time.
insights.quote: three-quarters of Student List supporters favour closer relations with the EU rather than Russia
insights.locator: A new opening for Serbia's EU accession talks?

insights.claim: Vučić's exit points to withdrawal of Serbian political support for Bosnian Serb nationalist Milorad Dodik and potentially improved relations with Montenegro, though none of this is guaranteed.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Lower Serbian backing for Republika Srpska separatism would reduce Bosnian political risk; monitor Belgrade's statements on Dodik.
insights.quote: None of those changes is guaranteed.

insights.claim: Serbia has a historic opportunity to rebuild its regional standing and be a driver of economic growth and political integration in the Balkans, provided its new leaders agree on direction.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Positive regional rerating hinges on governing cohesion rather than the election result alone.

insights.claim: The Student List faces a paradox: its decentralised organisation enabled rapid growth but governing requires clearer leadership and collective discipline, and most of its representatives have little or no government experience.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Execution and cohesion risk is the main source of downside to the reform thesis.
insights.quote: what got them so far will only get them so far
insights.locator: The harder test is yet to come

insights.claim: The new government must confront entrenched networks of the outgoing ruling party in public institutions, as in Hungary, while presidential elections are due before year-end and a stable parliamentary majority must hold through the first difficult policy decisions.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Near-term catalysts are the presidential vote, prime minister choice and early policy splits; the PM is still unknown, with former central bank governor Dejan Šoškić mentioned.
insights.locator: The harder test is yet to come
